items.title: NM3 designs "truly classic bar for Milan"
items.text: NM3 designs "truly classic bar for Milan" Magazine Awards Jobs Events Guide Showroom School Shows Courses Competitions Follow: Architecture Interiors Design Technology Series Features Interviews Opinion News Lookbooks Talks Videos Podcasts About Comments Newsletters Preferences Submit a story Advertise Privacy notice Contact Dezeen Magazine dezeen-logo dezeen-logo Next story clear Search --> --> Follow: Awards Jobs Events Guide Showroom School Shows Courses Competitions Series Interviews Opinion Talks Videos Newsletters Podcasts Magazine Architecture Interiors Design Technology --> Search results: Read more: Posts: --> Refine your search: Cats NM3 designs "truly classic bar for Milan" Share: Prefer Dezeen on Google Jane Englefield | 19 October 2026 Local studio NM3 looked to Vienna's iconic 20th-century American Bar by Adolf Loos when designing the bespoke red-hued interior of Milan's Bar Bardo. When designing the project, NM3 drew on the influential design of Loos's famous bar , an early modernist landmark finished in 1908. Bar Bardo was designed by NM3 "The American Bar was more of an aspiration than a direct formal reference," studio co-founder Francesco Zorzi told Dezeen. "The ambition was never to recreate Loos's bar, nor Robert and Trix Haussmann's Kronenhalle in Zurich, which was another important reference for the project," he explained. "Rather, we wanted to create a truly classic bar for Milan, with a very specific spatial and architectural character." The studio was informed by Adolf Loos's famous American Bar in Vienna Located just across the road from the city's popular Bar Basso , Bar Bardo is housed within a 55-square-metre single room with an additional bathroom. Almost every element in the listening bar was custom-designed by NM3, known for its modernist-style stainless steel furniture that has already made the young studio a household name in Milan since its founding in 2020. Polished rosewood panels clad the walls and ceilings The walls and ceiling were clad with polished rosewood panels, which add character to the small space while improving its acoustics. A quintessentially NM3 stainless steel bar was placed in the centre of the room, where its gleaming surfaces reflect the globular 1950s pendant lights by Italian architect Luigi Caccia Dominioni. The lamps are the only vintage pieces in the bar. NM3 swapped their original chains with longer black ones. Read: Dezeen's favourite wooden furniture and lighting from January The perimeter of the space features built-in red velvet banquette seating, which matches crimson curtains and a series of bright red speakers fitted across the bar to accommodate a stainless steel DJ booth and metal shelving for vinyl records. Bar Bardo was purposefully designed to be a flexible space. Every interior element is movable, with the exception of the bar and the banquettes. items.title: Traditional Thai lanterns inform blue-and-gold Bangkok cafe interior
items.text: Traditional Thai lanterns inform blue-and-gold Bangkok cafe interior Magazine Awards Jobs Events Guide Showroom School Shows Courses Competitions Follow: Architecture Interiors Design Technology Series Features Interviews Opinion News Lookbooks Talks Videos Podcasts About Comments Newsletters Preferences Submit a story Advertise Privacy notice Contact Dezeen Magazine dezeen-logo dezeen-logo Next story clear Search --> --> Follow: Awards Jobs Events Guide Showroom School Shows Courses Competitions Series Interviews Opinion Talks Videos Newsletters Podcasts Magazine Architecture Interiors Design Technology --> Search results: Read more: Posts: --> Refine your search: Cats Traditional Thai lanterns inform blue-and-gold Bangkok cafe interior Share: Prefer Dezeen on Google Cajsa Carlson | 19 October 2026 Japanese studio I IN drew on traditional Thai festivals, where thousands of paper lanterns are released into the sky, when creating the interior for the first Blue Bottle Coffee cafe in Bangkok . The interior of the cafe is dominated by the large Blue Lantern installation above the coffee counter. A "Blue Lantern" takes centre stage in this Bangkok cafe "The main idea came from Thailand's traditional lantern festival," I IN co-founder Yohei Terui told Dezeen. "We wanted to capture the feeling of a lantern floating in the sky and bring that into the space in a contemporary way." "This became what we call the Blue Lantern, a large sculptural element extending from the ceiling above the drip station," he continued. I IN wanted to create a dramatic design As it is the brand's first cafe in Bangkok, the studio wanted to design a "bold and dramatic" space that would also nod to local culture. "The lantern idea came from the local culture, and from the beginning, we wanted to make it as large and impactful as possible," Terui said. "We placed it at the location where customers first enter the cafe, so it would immediately catch their attention and become a symbol of the store." Teak was used for the fixtures and furniture The furniture and fixtures in the 178-square-metre cafe were made from teak wood, a material that is often avoided in the West due to concerns about illegal logging , but which is local to Thailand. "Every country has their own approach to natural materials, depending on what is locally available and traditionally used," Terui said. "In Thailand, especially in the north, teak is a very familiar material and commonly used in the interiors and architecture." Read: I IN contrasts concrete architecture with bright colours in Andersson Bell Tokyo store Blue Bottle Coffee cafe Bangkok is drenched in blue hues, with the brand's signature colour used for the lantern and coffee counter. For the rest of the space, I IN chose a pale blue colour to "give guests a sense of brand identity and the feeling of a sky," Terui explained. items.title: Gundry & Ducker draws on French dining culture for London restaurant Cassette
items.text: Gundry & Ducker draws on French dining culture for Cassette Magazine Awards Jobs Events Guide Showroom School Shows Courses Competitions Follow: Architecture Interiors Design Technology Series Features Interviews Opinion News Lookbooks Talks Videos Podcasts About Comments Newsletters Preferences Submit a story Advertise Privacy notice Contact Dezeen Magazine dezeen-logo dezeen-logo Next story clear Search --> --> Follow: Awards Jobs Events Guide Showroom School Shows Courses Competitions Series Interviews Opinion Talks Videos Newsletters Podcasts Magazine Architecture Interiors Design Technology --> Search results: Read more: Posts: --> Refine your search: Cats Gundry & Ducker draws on French dining culture for London restaurant Cassette Share: Prefer Dezeen on Google Rachael Gilby | 12 October 2026 Design studio Gundry & Ducker has renovated the interiors of a Grade II-listed workshop for Cassette, a Parisian-style bistro that has recently opened in the heart of London 's West End. The spacious eatery is housed within a nineteenth-century gothic building, which features double-height ceilings and an expansive glass facade with intricate detailing. The design was informed by traditional Parisian bistros Located in Covent Garden, the restaurant spans 107 square metres and accommodates 52 customers across a ground floor dining room and a basement level. An outdoor terrace welcomes an additional 30 guests when the weather permits. "Our brief talked about a neighbourhood restaurant in the centre of town," Gundry & Ducker co-founder Tyeth Gundry told Dezeen. "From there, the conversation centred on familiarity, recognition and ease – creating a neighbourhood restaurant for friends who live in different parts of the city." The studio chose a warm, neutral colour palette for the interior The studio intended for the design to resemble traditional Parisian establishments by incorporating familiar elements, including deep aubergine finishes, dark banquette seating and classic bentwood bistro chairs. Alongside this, the designers combined natural fabrics, sapele wood and stainless steel with exposed brickwork to create a restrained colour palette and an overall "deliberately unfussy" interior. The design combines a mixture of dark woods with natural fabrics and stainless steel "We talked a lot about colour: summer park landscapes, Parisian bistros and wine," Gundry explained. "Tone too was really important; we needed colours that would dim well to help us create a low-level evening setting that feels warm; the key to which is controlling reflected light," he continued. The Grade II-listed interior has double-height ceilings and a large glass facade Taking cues from the surrounding theatre district, the studio installed a sophisticated sound system and a statement curtain with acoustic qualities that wraps around the main dining area. items.title: Formant Studio reinterprets the classic tavern at contemporary Mexico City restaurant
items.text: Formant Studio designs Nota restaurant in Mexico City Magazine Awards Jobs Events Guide Showroom School Shows Courses Competitions Follow: Architecture Interiors Design Technology Series Features Interviews Opinion News Lookbooks Talks Videos Podcasts About Comments Newsletters Preferences Submit a story Advertise Privacy notice Contact Dezeen Magazine dezeen-logo dezeen-logo Next story clear Search --> --> Follow: Awards Jobs Events Guide Showroom School Shows Courses Competitions Series Interviews Opinion Talks Videos Newsletters Podcasts Magazine Architecture Interiors Design Technology --> Search results: Read more: Posts: --> Refine your search: Cats Formant Studio reinterprets the classic tavern at contemporary Mexico City restaurant Share: Prefer Dezeen on Google Ben Dreith | 9 October 2026 Local practice Formant Studio created custom furniture and fixtures while designing Mexico City restaurant Nota Tavern, taking references from classic Chicago taverns in the fit-out of a former residence. Located in the city's Escandón I neighbourhood, Nota Tavern is a two-storey Italian-American restaurant. It sits on a site that once held a hacienda-style residence that was converted into an apartment building, with the owner preserving half of the original house. The restaurant sits in this portion. Formant Studio designed the interiors and most of the furniture at Nota Tavern in Mexico City Formant Studio was tasked with translating the design of classic Chicago taverns into a contemporary mode. "The main request was to create a faithful interpretation of the neighbourhood taverns of Chicago – the kind of places built less around spectacle and more around familiarity," Formant Studio co-founder Alejandro Valencia told Dezeen. "The design translates the character of a classic tavern into a contemporary architectural language." The two-storey restaurant serves Italian-American cuisine Valencia also said the studio took other cues from Chicago and integrated the clean minimalism of Ludwig Mies van der Rohe and the warmer modernism of Frank Lloyd Wright , both architects known for their work in the US city. Also in the tradition of the 20th-century modern architects, Formant Studio designed most of the furniture, from the black-stained oak tables to the steel bar stools and sleek metal sconces. The space was once a hacienda-style residence and its original columns were preserved and restored The majority of the dining room was clad in Mexican rosewood panels, which also form the custom banquettes upholstered in black Kvadrat textiles. Formant Studio said that the previous space defined how it organised the restaurant. Mexican rosewood covers the walls and forms banquette seating The current space still has ornate stone pillars that once framed an entrance portico. items.title: Josh Greenspan creates New York cocktail lounge almost entirely with USM modules
items.text: This cocktail lounge was made almost entirely from USM modules Magazine Awards Jobs Events Guide Showroom School Shows Courses Competitions Follow: Architecture Interiors Design Technology Series Features Interviews Opinion News Lookbooks Talks Videos Podcasts About Comments Newsletters Preferences Submit a story Advertise Privacy notice Contact Dezeen Magazine dezeen-logo dezeen-logo Next story clear Search --> --> Follow: Awards Jobs Events Guide Showroom School Shows Courses Competitions Series Interviews Opinion Talks Videos Newsletters Podcasts Magazine Architecture Interiors Design Technology --> Search results: Read more: Posts: --> Refine your search: Cats Josh Greenspan creates New York cocktail lounge almost entirely with USM modules Share: Prefer Dezeen on Google Ellen Eberhardt | 8 October 2026 Restaurateur Josh Greenspan and furniture company USM have created VV's Cocktail Room in Manhattan, a small space wrapped almost entirely in Steel Blue USM Haller modular shelving and informed by Greenspan's visits to Japan and Hong Kong . Named after Greenspan 's daughter Vivienne, VV's Cocktail Room (VV's) is located in Chelsea and contains just 18 seats to mimic the intimacy of an omakase cocktail experience, where bartenders lead a multi-course tasting or cocktail menu. Josh Greenspan and USM have completed Manhattan cocktail bar VV's Cocktail Room The project stems from Greenspan's ongoing conversations with USM, which frequently collaborates with designers to outfit spaces and create installations from the flexible panelling system. "I started imagining something a little wild – a space built entirely from the USM system, pushing its modularity in unexpected ways," Greenspan told Dezeen. "I'm thrilled that the USM team embraced the idea and came along for the ride." The space is wrapped in a dark blue USM Haller System Visitors to the bar pass a glass block wall partition to enter the space. Inside, navy blue USM panels form the walls that surround the space and wrap behind the bar, where they jut out into shelving. A dark walnut wood was used for the bar top and tables, which is offset by bar seats upholstered in a burgundy fabric and banquette seating built by Greenspan's father, Michael Greenspan, covered in a similar hue. Read: Norwegian designers use reclaimed materials to customise USM Haller furniture Other details include a wavy pendant light by New York lighting studio Studio Kawabi that spans the length of the bar and a painting by Japanese artist Keita Morimoto affixed to the back wall. The space was informed by the "visual language" of Tokyo and Hong Kong, according to the team, and aims for the futuristic aesthetic between the 1960s and 1990s of the two metropolises. items.title: Spirit of Iberian taverns informs wood-heavy Parisian restaurant
items.text: Spirit of Iberian taverns informs wood-heavy Parisian restaurant Magazine Awards Jobs Events Guide Showroom School Shows Courses Competitions Follow: Architecture Interiors Design Technology Series Features Interviews Opinion News Lookbooks Talks Videos Podcasts About Comments Newsletters Preferences Submit a story Advertise Privacy notice Contact Dezeen Magazine dezeen-logo dezeen-logo Next story clear Search --> --> Follow: Awards Jobs Events Guide Showroom School Shows Courses Competitions Series Interviews Opinion Talks Videos Newsletters Podcasts Magazine Architecture Interiors Design Technology --> Search results: Read more: Posts: --> Refine your search: Cats Spirit of Iberian taverns informs wood-heavy Parisian restaurant Share: Prefer Dezeen on Google Jane Englefield | 6 October 2026 Emerging Marseille firm Bétyle Studio has designed the interiors for Arcane 17, a Basque and Catalan restaurant in Paris featuring patinated timber and distinctive marquetry . Located in the city's Le Marais neighbourhood in the 4th arrondissement, Arcane 17 is a petite eatery that sits within a centuries-old building. Arcane 17 is a Basque and Catalan restaurant Bétyle Studio founders Carla Romano and Nicolas Cazenave de la Roche wanted to honour the owners' Catalan roots through their restaurant design. "Rather than reproducing the codes of a traditional Spanish restaurant, we wanted to reinterpret the idea of the Iberian tavern through a more contemporary and refined language," studio founders Carla Romano and Nicolas Cazenave de la Roche told Dezeen. Bétyle Studio designed the interiors for the space In this spirit, the designers clad the open space in an abundance of wood. The dining area is characterised by ebonised panelling, while the tubular stainless steel bar is topped with delicate slabs of marquetry detailing playful motifs, from shooting stars to a cartoonish lobster. Classic bentwood chairs make up the dining space "We drew inspiration from the energy of rural churches, dark woods and the movement of traditional fans," explained Romano and Cazenave de la Roche. "We did not want these references to be literal, but rather to emerge through materials, textures and forms." Classic, bentwood chairs feature alongside uniform timber tables. In one corner, a red-clad banquette subtly nods to traditional Parisian bistros. Read: Gjergji Shkurti integrates bar, retail and hi-fi at Million Goods in Brooklyn All of the space's joinery was conceived bespoke for the restaurant by a Marseille-based carpenter and frequent collaborator of Bétyle Studio. "We worked with different species of wood and experimented with various techniques to stain, ebonise and patinate the timber," said Romano and Cazenave de la Roche. "The idea was to give depth to the surfaces and create elements that feel as though they could have belonged to the space for a long time." items.text: Bar Shrimp uses laser-etched acoustic panels to balance music and conversation Magazine Awards Jobs Events Guide Showroom School Shows Courses Competitions Follow: Architecture Interiors Design Technology Series Features Interviews Opinion News Lookbooks Talks Videos Podcasts About Comments Newsletters Preferences Submit a story Advertise Privacy notice Contact Dezeen Magazine dezeen-logo dezeen-logo Next story clear Search --> --> Follow: Awards Jobs Events Guide Showroom School Shows Courses Competitions Series Interviews Opinion Talks Videos Newsletters Podcasts Magazine Architecture Interiors Design Technology --> Search results: Read more: Posts: --> Refine your search: Cats Bar Shrimp uses laser-etched acoustic panels to balance music and conversation Share: Prefer Dezeen on Google Francesca Tesler | 6 October 2026 Cocktail bar and restaurant Bar Shrimp combines red velvet interiors with bespoke acoustic panels from Autex Acoustics to balance music and conversation, shown in this video produced by Dezeen. Located in Manchester , Bar Shrimp has a custom sound system and a dark interior with floor-to-ceiling red velvet curtains and plush banquettes, reminiscent of vintage New York bars and music lounges. The design was informed by the founders' experience of bars around the world, where co-founder Richard Cossins said they were struck by ones with particularly good sound. "When we first saw the space, we wanted to create a relaxed and comfortable environment, where guests could spend numerous hours within the space," Cossins told Dezeen. Bar Shrimp's interior draws on mid-century bar decor The existing space had a concrete floor and glass walls, prompting the team to introduce softer materials to improve the acoustics. Autex Acoustics worked with the team from an early stage, supplying a bespoke Frontier Axis ceiling system and Mirage wall panels to reduce reverberation and echo. The acoustic treatment was designed to complement the interior rather than disappear into it, with laser-etched patterns giving the Mirage panels a textured finish inspired by natural materials. DJs provide a curated music programme throughout the day "We're looking at it from a technical perspective, but also from an aesthetic perspective," said Autex Acoustics UK, EU and the Middle East director Daniel Senior. "We laser etch a pattern into a panel," he continued. "That allows us to create some really intricate designs, to create real depth and texture to a panel, all taking inspiration from natural materials." Bar Shrimp also features a custom MasterSounds Clarity M-1215 Audio system – a large-format modular speaker system designed to provide high-quality sound throughout the space. The panels were chosen to blend with the rest of the restaurant's interior. Cossins said the acoustic treatment was intended to make the bar comfortable even when music is playing at a high volume. items.title: Luxury ocean liners inform New York's Kimpton Era hotel by INC
items.text: Luxury ocean liners inform New York's Kimpton Era hotel by INC Magazine Awards Jobs Events Guide Showroom School Shows Courses Competitions Follow: Architecture Interiors Design Technology Series Features Interviews Opinion News Lookbooks Talks Videos Podcasts About Comments Newsletters Preferences Submit a story Advertise Privacy notice Contact Dezeen Magazine dezeen-logo dezeen-logo Next story clear Search --> --> Follow: Awards Jobs Events Guide Showroom School Shows Courses Competitions Series Interviews Opinion Talks Videos Newsletters Podcasts Magazine Architecture Interiors Design Technology --> Search results: Read more: Posts: --> Refine your search: Cats Luxury ocean liners inform New York's Kimpton Era hotel by INC Share: Prefer Dezeen on Google Dan Howarth | 3 October 2026 Local architecture studio INC has designed each guest room at this hotel overlooking New York 's Rockefeller Plaza to emulate "a stateroom on an ocean liner". The 529-key Kimpton Era is housed within a purpose-built, 33-storey tower on West 48th Street, just south of the art deco Rockefeller Center complex. The Kimpton Era's blackened-steel staircase spirals up through a three-storey fluted atrium For the interiors, INC pulled in references from New York City itself, blending Uptown elegance and Downtown grit, as well as the compact grandeur of the luxury liners that once docked along the Hudson. "Every detail of the Kimpton Era is engineered elegance with a room that feels more like a stateroom on an ocean liner – compact, crafted, and refined to the luxury of just enough," said INC partner Adam Rolston. The reception area is anchored by a tiered black-stone counter Materials throughout were chosen to reflect the city's dichotomy, pairing marbles, brass, leather and glazed ceramics with more industrial concrete and blackened steel. In a triple-height atrium wrapped in fluted concrete, a blackened steel-and-glass stair coils around a mobile of organic forms that descends from the ceiling. The second-floor brasserie featured panelled walls and mosaic flooring Cerused wood, terrazzo borders and diffused lighting define the elevator lobbies, while the tiered black-marble reception counter provides a weighted presence. "Inspired by the city itself, the Kimpton Era captures New York's layered character — elegant yet gritty, refined yet raw – woven into a vertical voyage of venues and comfort in a purpose-built skyscraper at the heart of Rockefeller Center," said INC's Hillary Kroll. Terracotta-toned walls and ceramic pendants add texture in the restaurant spanning the ground and cellar levels The hotel's five dining venues include a Latin American eatery with terracotta walls and ceramic pendants that spans from the ground floor to the cellar. A second-floor brasserie features banquette seating, panelled walls, a scarlet ceramic bar and mosaic floors, while the third-floor lobby cafe offers coffee in the mornings and cocktails at night. items.title: Rezen transforms hotel stables in Australia into "raw and direct" wellness centre
items.text: Rezen transforms stables in Australia into Alchemy Saunas Magazine Awards Jobs Events Guide Showroom School Shows Courses Competitions Follow: Architecture Interiors Design Technology Series Features Interviews Opinion News Lookbooks Talks Videos Podcasts About Comments Newsletters Preferences Submit a story Advertise Privacy notice Contact Dezeen Magazine dezeen-logo dezeen-logo Next story clear Search --> --> Follow: Awards Jobs Events Guide Showroom School Shows Courses Competitions Series Interviews Opinion Talks Videos Newsletters Podcasts Magazine Architecture Interiors Design Technology --> Search results: Read more: Posts: --> Refine your search: Cats Rezen transforms hotel stables in Australia into "raw and direct" wellness centre Share: Prefer Dezeen on Google Jon Astbury | 28 September 2026 Arched openings and rough brick walls evoke the feel of a Roman bathhouse at Alchemy Saunas, a wellness centre in Australia by interior design studio Rezen. The project involved transforming a former stable and cellar at the base of the Royal George Hotel in Fremantle, which dates back to 1903 and is currently undergoing redevelopment. Rezen chose to highlight the existing red brick and local Tamala limestone surfaces of the existing space, complementing them with "utilitarian" additions in steel and tilework. Rezen has converted a former stable into Alchemy Saunas "Given its history as a space of utility, the project uses a design language which is pragmatic, raw and direct," studio director Rhys Bowring told Dezeen. "Philosophically, we wanted the new material palette to be recessive and allow the existing materiality to be the focal point," Bowring told Dezeen. "We also wanted to use materials that were not overly decorative, self-finishing and utilitarian in keeping with its original use." Existing rough brick walls line the wellness centre The layout of Alchemy Saunas was constrained by the fact that any new openings had to correspond to locations pre-approved for a previous hospitality project that was later abandoned. Entering via the hotel's basement, a steel staircase in the centre's reception leads up to the changing rooms and showers. These sit behind a stainless steel wall that starkly contrasts the original rough limestone walls. There are two pools alongside the saunas Alongside, a sauna has been tucked into the western corner of the plan, finished with glazing and tiles on its exterior and lined internally with pale timber. Another steel stair leads back down into the basement and two central pools – one an ice pool and the other a warm magnesium pool – which are positioned within the double-height volume of the former stable and are illuminated by large, arched windows. items.text: Gjergji Shkurti gives Millions Goods Ft Greene a regal renovation Magazine Awards Jobs Events Guide Showroom School Shows Courses Competitions Follow: Architecture Interiors Design Technology Series Features Interviews Opinion News Lookbooks Talks Videos Podcasts About Comments Newsletters Preferences Submit a story Advertise Privacy notice Contact Dezeen Magazine dezeen-logo dezeen-logo Next story clear Search --> --> Follow: Awards Jobs Events Guide Showroom School Shows Courses Competitions Series Interviews Opinion Talks Videos Newsletters Podcasts Magazine Architecture Interiors Design Technology --> Search results: Read more: Posts: --> Refine your search: Cats Gjergji Shkurti integrates bar, retail and hi-fi at Million Goods in Brooklyn Share: Prefer Dezeen on Google Ben Dreith | 25 September 2026 Architect Gjergji Shkurti has collaborated with concept shop Million Goods for its second Brooklyn location, using marble, custom millwork and curated furniture to create a transition from hospitality to retail. A glossy red spiral staircase can be spotted through windows that face the buzzy part of DeKalb Street in Fort Greene, Brooklyn. The space became the Million Goods 's second shop after co-founder Matt Reyer, who lives nearby, spotting it when it was inhabited by a design studio. Gjergji Shkurti designed the Fort Greene outpost for Million Goods Reyer and fellow co-founder Drew Kaufmann brought on local architect Gjergji Shkurti, founder of Figure Ground , to convert the space. Whereas the original Million Goods in Greenpoint is condensed into a single level, the Fort Greene location gave the team more room to work with, with two levels and an expansive courtyard. The studio revamped a two-level space "I think this was more regal, whereas Greenpoint was a little bit more fun," Shkurti told Dezeen, referring to the expansive Breccia Pernice stone countertop that forms the wine bar portion on the first level. Stripping the interiors back to their essentials, Shkurti organised the space to provide social areas and retail, integrating them stylistically but separating them physically, with the social spaces on the bottom floor and the retail above. Shkurti designed the space and fabricated the millwork The first-level bar and social space combines multiple different design languages into a contemporary New York style. Behind the bar, metallic speaker boxes were integrated into the custom casework, which was rendered in sapele wood finished in a peca tone. Bridge Street Sound did the sound system, integrating a large speaker directly into the face of the marble bar. Emeco bar stools by Philippe Starck line the bar, and these chairs were used with the wooden banquet seating that hems the space. A backyard takes cues from Brazilian brutalism The ceiling has a distinctly Japanese appearance, with fabric draped between wooden slats. items.title: Fritz Hansen Sound Club invites visitors to enjoy music in Bauhaus-inspired listening spaces
items.text: Fritz Hansen Sound Club features Bauhaus-style listening spaces Magazine Awards Jobs Events Guide Showroom School Shows Courses Competitions Follow: Architecture Interiors Design Technology Series Features Interviews Opinion News Lookbooks Talks Videos Podcasts About Comments Newsletters Preferences Submit a story Advertise Privacy notice Contact Dezeen Magazine dezeen-logo dezeen-logo Next story clear Search --> --> Follow: Awards Jobs Events Guide Showroom School Shows Courses Competitions Series Interviews Opinion Talks Videos Newsletters Podcasts Magazine Architecture Interiors Design Technology --> Search results: Read more: Posts: --> Refine your search: Cats Fritz Hansen Sound Club invites visitors to enjoy music in Bauhaus-inspired listening spaces Share: Prefer Dezeen on Google Alyn Griffiths | 20 September 2026 Danish design brand Fritz Hansen has teamed up with audio specialist Technics to transform its Farringdon showroom into a series of domestic listening scenes for London Design Festival . As part of the Fritz Hansen Sound Club, the showroom has been organised into four domestic scenes where guests are invited to listen to a curated selection of vinyl records. Fritz Hansen Sound Club held its latest edition during London Design Festival The installation combines Fritz Hansen's furniture and lighting products with turntables, headphones and speakers from Japanese firm Technics . A 90th anniversary limited edition of the Kaiser Idell Luxus table lamp and Technics' SL 40CBT turntable form the centrepiece of the various settings, both reimagined in a matching burgundy hue. The installation invited visitors to listen to a selection of vinyl records In reference to the table lamp's modernist origins, the interior styling evokes the Bauhaus movement and combines 1930s furniture with pieces from Fritz Hansen's catalogue. Fritz Hansen Sound Club originally debuted during 3 Days of Design in Copenhagen, with the aim to explore how sound informs the way users experience interior settings. It featured a special burgundy edition of the Kaiser Idell Luxus table lamp "Sound plays a direct role in how we experience space," said Fritz Hansen creative director, Els Van Hoorebeeck. "It shapes how we move, where we pause, and how we relate to furniture, light and materials." "With Fritz Hansen Sound Club, we explore how these elements work together to define the character of a space, and how this way of thinking continues to shape our design today." Read: London design "an international success story" says Sadiq Khan The Study area pairs steel-framed desks with Arne Jacobsen's Ant Chair in a cherry veneer finish, while the designer's iconic Egg Chair provides a cosy spot for relaxing in the nearby Reading Corner. Downstairs, the Living Room provides a setting for socialising, with a turntable and speakers oriented towards the guests. items.title: Seven interiors where billiard tables are available on cue
items.text: Seven interiors where billiard tables are available on cue Magazine Awards Jobs Events Guide Showroom School Shows Courses Competitions Follow: Architecture Interiors Design Technology Series Features Interviews Opinion News Lookbooks Talks Videos Podcasts About Comments Newsletters Preferences Submit a story Advertise Privacy notice Contact Dezeen Magazine dezeen-logo dezeen-logo Next story clear Search --> --> Follow: Awards Jobs Events Guide Showroom School Shows Courses Competitions Series Interviews Opinion Talks Videos Newsletters Podcasts Magazine Architecture Interiors Design Technology --> Search results: Read more: Posts: --> Refine your search: Cats Seven interiors where billiard tables are available on cue Share: Prefer Dezeen on Google Alice Laycock | 13 September 2026 From bars and hotels to private homes , this lookbook explores interiors where billiard tables are on hand for spontaneous games. Billiard tables – comprising a cloth-covered surface surrounded by cushioned sides that are punctuated with netted pockets – are a type of table that cue sports can be played on, such as pool and snooker. While they are traditionally covered in dark green cloth, to recall the appearance of grass lawns, contemporary designs feature differently-coloured cloth, from blues and reds to neutrals. Brightly coloured balls make the tables instantly recognisable, standing out against the background cloth when contained in a triangular rack or strewn around the table mid-play. The following interiors all feature billiard tables, from traditional games rooms in hospitality venues to unconventional placements in residential kitchens and living rooms. This is the latest in our lookbooks series, which provides visual inspiration from Dezeen's archive. For more inspiration, see previous lookbooks featuring wooden staircases , picture windows and cottage living rooms . Photo by Christopher Sturman Soho House São Paulo, Brazil, by Soho House Sculptural legs, deep netted pockets and a navy top allow this monolithic billiard table to anchor a lofty games room in members' club Soho House 's São Paulo outpost. Its ornately inlayed base ties it in with pattern found elsewhere in the room, from wall hangings to lounge chairs. Find out more about Soho House São Paulo › Photo courtesy of Caceres + Tous House Kala, Indonesia, by Caceres + Tous When the panoramic jungle and sea views have been taken in, residents of this home on the Indonesian island of Lombok can retreat indoors for a game of pool. Within a black-painted room, a billiard table with a honey-coloured wooden base and a pale, sandy-coloured tabletop allows the multicoloured balls to stand out. items.title: Luxury ocean liners inform New York's Kimpton Era hotel by INC
items.text: Luxury ocean liners inform New York's Kimpton Era hotel by INC Magazine Awards Jobs Events Guide Showroom School Shows Courses Competitions Follow: Architecture Interiors Design Technology Series Features Interviews Opinion News Lookbooks Talks Videos Podcasts About Comments Newsletters Preferences Submit a story Advertise Privacy notice Contact Dezeen Magazine dezeen-logo dezeen-logo Next story clear Search --> --> Follow: Awards Jobs Events Guide Showroom School Shows Courses Competitions Series Interviews Opinion Talks Videos Newsletters Podcasts Magazine Architecture Interiors Design Technology --> Search results: Read more: Posts: --> Refine your search: Cats Luxury ocean liners inform New York's Kimpton Era hotel by INC Share: Prefer Dezeen on Google Dan Howarth | 3 October 2026 Local architecture studio INC has designed each guest room at this hotel overlooking New York 's Rockefeller Plaza to emulate "a stateroom on an ocean liner". The 529-key Kimpton Era is housed within a purpose-built, 33-storey tower on West 48th Street, just south of the art deco Rockefeller Center complex. The Kimpton Era's blackened-steel staircase spirals up through a three-storey fluted atrium For the interiors, INC pulled in references from New York City itself, blending Uptown elegance and Downtown grit, as well as the compact grandeur of the luxury liners that once docked along the Hudson. "Every detail of the Kimpton Era is engineered elegance with a room that feels more like a stateroom on an ocean liner – compact, crafted, and refined to the luxury of just enough," said INC partner Adam Rolston. The reception area is anchored by a tiered black-stone counter Materials throughout were chosen to reflect the city's dichotomy, pairing marbles, brass, leather and glazed ceramics with more industrial concrete and blackened steel. In a triple-height atrium wrapped in fluted concrete, a blackened steel-and-glass stair coils around a mobile of organic forms that descends from the ceiling. The second-floor brasserie featured panelled walls and mosaic flooring Cerused wood, terrazzo borders and diffused lighting define the elevator lobbies, while the tiered black-marble reception counter provides a weighted presence. "Inspired by the city itself, the Kimpton Era captures New York's layered character — elegant yet gritty, refined yet raw – woven into a vertical voyage of venues and comfort in a purpose-built skyscraper at the heart of Rockefeller Center," said INC's Hillary Kroll. Terracotta-toned walls and ceramic pendants add texture in the restaurant spanning the ground and cellar levels The hotel's five dining venues include a Latin American eatery with terracotta walls and ceramic pendants that spans from the ground floor to the cellar. A second-floor brasserie features banquette seating, panelled walls, a scarlet ceramic bar and mosaic floors, while the third-floor lobby cafe offers coffee in the mornings and cocktails at night. items.title: Raised walkway ties together 360‑metre-long hotel
items.text: Raised walkway ties together 360‑metre-long hotel Magazine Awards Jobs Events Guide Showroom School Shows Courses Competitions Follow: Architecture Interiors Design Technology Series Features Interviews Opinion News Lookbooks Talks Videos Podcasts About Comments Newsletters Preferences Submit a story Advertise Privacy notice Contact Dezeen Magazine dezeen-logo dezeen-logo Next story clear Search --> --> Follow: Awards Jobs Events Guide Showroom School Shows Courses Competitions Series Interviews Opinion Talks Videos Newsletters Podcasts Magazine Architecture Interiors Design Technology --> Search results: Read more: Posts: --> Refine your search: Cats Raised walkway ties together 360‑metre-long hotel Share: Prefer Dezeen on Google Kaia Wang | 29 September 2026 Chinese studios HB Architects and Nature Times Art have completed a hotel in Jiashan, China , which is connected by a 360-metre-long raised walkway. Named Dayun Landison Manor, the hotel occupies the elongated site of a demolished village. It stretches 360-metre-long from east to west, with a maximum width of 54 metres in the middle that narrows to 21 metres at the ends. HB Architects and Nature Times Art have completed a hotel in Jiashan The hotel is formed of numerous buildings connected by a walkway raised 4.9 metres above ground. According to the studios, this horizontal layout is a nod to the history of the site and an attempt to recreate a village-like neighbourhood. "We fictionalised a village to continue the functional essence of 'dwelling'," HB Architects and Nature Times Art told Dezeen. Terracotta red and earthy yellow are used as the main colours of this building The raised guest rooms were also designed to reference local housing, which is often supported on pilotis. However, the columns supporting the structures were deliberately hidden to highlight the visual dominance of the horizontal slab that runs through the site. The slab is 1.1 metres thick and sits 4.9 metres above the ground The hotel's entrance opens into a courtyard with a lake at its centre and a "water curtain" that falls from surrounding walkway. Guests then walk up stairs to the raised walkway that passes around courtyards and gardens to get to the rooms. A large pool occupies the tip at one end of the raised platform. "The building offers more than just one kind of experience," said the studios. "You have to walk through it yourself to really get it." Read: Hotel Wuxi MGallery Collection informed by historical poet's home While the rooms are arranged in blocks surrounding the raised walkway, more functional spaces were placed below the slab. The upper blocks were painted earthy yellow, while the lower floor and walkways were painted terracotta red as a reference to the surrounding landscape. Courtyards allow nature to permeate throughout the building "We deliberately chose to avoid white buildings," said HB Architects and Nature Times Art. "The colours we use in this building show how we think about nature."

items.title: SODA transforms hostel into "design-conscious" pod hotel
items.text: SODA creates "design-conscious" Otherwander pod hotel Magazine Awards Jobs Events Guide Showroom School Shows Courses Competitions Follow: Architecture Interiors Design Technology Series Features Interviews Opinion News Lookbooks Talks Videos Podcasts About Comments Newsletters Preferences Submit a story Advertise Privacy notice Contact Dezeen Magazine dezeen-logo dezeen-logo Next story clear Search --> --> Follow: Awards Jobs Events Guide Showroom School Shows Courses Competitions Series Interviews Opinion Talks Videos Newsletters Podcasts Magazine Architecture Interiors Design Technology --> Search results: Read more: Posts: --> Refine your search: Cats SODA transforms hostel into "design-conscious" pod hotel Share: Prefer Dezeen on Google Lizzie Crook | 27 September 2026 London studio SODA has converted a backpacker hostel into Otherwander Soho, a high-density capsule hotel in central London with vibrantly-coloured social spaces. Otherwander combines 566 sleeping pods, or "nests", with shared social spaces, targeted at young travellers and those seeking budget-friendly city-centre accommodation. It occupies a former hostel housed across a pair of early 20th-century buildings close to Oxford Street, transformed and expanded by SODA . SODA has created the Otherwander capsule hotel in Soho "The aim was to provide affordable, high-density accommodation without compromising the guest experience," SODA director Ryan Holland told Dezeen. "The original target demographic was primarily Gen Z and younger independent travellers who are design-conscious and prioritise location and experience," Holland continued. "However, our intention was always to create a design which felt inclusive to all demographics, and we’re now finding that the hotel has a much broader appeal to all sorts of age groups who equally want well-designed, affordable accommodation in central London." It contains 566 sleeping pods Pod hotels, also known as capsule hotels, are affordable, ultra-compact accommodation comprising rows of small stacked sleeping spaces and shared bathroom and social areas, rather than traditional ensuite rooms. They are often associated with Japan, where the first example opened in Osaka in 1979. They are now becoming increasingly common in cities around the world. Visitors enter through a glossy lobby with e-gates "Pods make central city locations more affordable in a city where space and hotel costs are exceptionally high," said Holland. "The model particularly suits short stays and travellers who intend to experience the city rather than spend significant time in their room." Social spaces are located on the ground floor SODA oversaw both the architecture and interiors of the project. It focused on preserving, retaining and connecting the pair of heritage buildings on Dean Street, while adding a rear extension that felt contemporary yet in keeping with the area. items.title: Grand Ji Hotel debuts at Paris Design Week
items.text: Grand Ji Hotel debuts at Paris Design Week Magazine Awards Jobs Events Guide Showroom School Shows Courses Competitions Follow: Architecture Interiors Design Technology Series Features Interviews Opinion News Lookbooks Talks Videos Podcasts About Comments Newsletters Preferences Submit a story Advertise Privacy notice Contact Dezeen Magazine dezeen-logo dezeen-logo Next story clear Search --> --> Follow: Awards Jobs Events Guide Showroom School Shows Courses Competitions Series Interviews Opinion Talks Videos Newsletters Podcasts Magazine Architecture Interiors Design Technology --> Search results: Read more: Posts: --> Refine your search: Cats Grand Ji Hotel debuts at Paris Design Week Share: Prefer Dezeen on Google Dezeen staff | 18 September 2026 Promotion: H World has debuted its latest hotel brand, the Grand Ji Hotel, in Hangzhou, China , designed by Chinese studio Vermilion Zhou Design Group, which aims to reinvent hotel design through its dedication to symbolic ritual. Grand Ji Hotel, a premium brand under H World Group , has made its official debut at Paris Design Week's China Creative Power (CCP) pavilion as an official annual partner, taking place from 10 to 19 September. The hotel's spatial design was led by Kuang Ming (Ray) Chou, founder and creative director of Vermilion Zhou Design Group and chief designer of H World Group. H World debuted its Grand Ji Hotel during Paris Design Week According to H World, Grand Ji Hotel draws on the phrase "the formless greatness, a quiet way of seeing" and is informed by the Taoist concept of 大象无形, which suggests that the most powerful forms are often "quiet and insular". Instead of an overtly luxurious look, the hotel's aesthetic is described as "quiet, yet possessed of presence, unlayered, yet full of depth". The technology woven into the design ensures the guest experience is seamless Rather than weaving traditional Chinese imagery throughout the hotel design, Grand Ji Hotel was designed to break the conventional hotel paradigms and instead focus on quietly enhancing visitor experience. For example, the way guests arrive, dine, rest and depart are treated as part of one integrated system. When guests arrive, instead of checking in at a large front desk, they are greeted by a tea table where they can first enjoy a tea ceremony and a hot cup of tea. Guests are greeted with a tea ceremony upon arrival At Grand Ji Hotels, technology is integrated purposefully into the background to ensure a smooth experience. Visitors can use their phones as a room key, and rooms are also fitted with innovative control systems, where curtains, televisions, and air conditioning are controlled via voice commands. H World explained that the "Eastern spirit" is woven into each room's design, with furniture that evokes a sense of sensory calm and hospitality rituals embedded in the structure. Set to be built in Tomakomai City, the Poké Ball-Themed Hotel will feature a three-metre-diameter spherical guest room shaped like the balls used to catch and store wild creatures in the popular Pokémon game. Not A Hotel has announced it will open a guest room shaped like a giant Poké Ball Designed by Not A Hotel 's in-house team of architects, the structure will comprise two moulded acrylic hemispheres and a curved acrylic window, giving the appearance of an opening ball. It will aim to immerse guests in both the natural setting and the world of Pokémon. It will be situated on a lakeside in Hokkaido Visitors will enter the spherical structure through a sliding, curved door. Inside, a custom-designed circular mattress will fill most of the interior. A washroom will be decorated in tiles the colour of the Snorlax – a Pokémon character known for its long sleeping habits. Guests will be able to select custom interior lighting themes based on Pokémon characters. Read: Iittala and Pokémon design stripy tableware emblazoned with Pikachu "As society becomes increasingly convenient and efficient, Not A Hotel aims to bring more joy to individuals' lives," said Not A Hotel. "For years, Pokémon fans have dreamed of stepping inside a Poké Ball," it continued. "Not A Hotel, leveraging its architectural and technological expertise, has turned that dream into a reality." "This structure transcends the boundaries of architecture and product design, fusing the world of Pokémon with the architectural quality that defines Not A Hotel." A circular mattress will fill the space Created in collaboration with sleep-tracking game app Pokémon Sleep , the hotel will open in celebration of the third anniversary of Pokémon Sleep and the 30th anniversary of Pokémon this year. Not A Hotel said people will get the chance to stay in the giant poké ball by winning an upcoming competition, but the room will not open to the public for bookings or visits. items.text: Orms to add rooftop pool to London's BT Tower Magazine Awards Jobs Events Guide Showroom School Shows Courses Competitions Follow: Architecture Interiors Design Technology Series Features Interviews Opinion News Lookbooks Talks Videos Podcasts About Comments Newsletters Preferences Submit a story Advertise Privacy notice Contact Dezeen Magazine dezeen-logo dezeen-logo Next story clear Search --> --> Follow: Awards Jobs Events Guide Showroom School Shows Courses Competitions Series Interviews Opinion Talks Videos Newsletters Podcasts Magazine Architecture Interiors Design Technology --> Search results: Read more: Posts: --> Refine your search: Cats Orms plans to add rooftop swimming pool to London's BT Tower Share: Prefer Dezeen on Google Amy Peacock | 10 September 2026 Architecture studio Orms has submitted a planning application to transform the BT Tower in London into a hotel with a rooftop swimming pool for American hotelier MCR. Orms will restore the Grade II-listed BT Tower, the adjacent podium and 1930s Howland Building, and convert the complex into a hotel with ground-floor shops, bars and restaurants, if the application is approved by the London Borough of Camden. A publicly accessible swimming pool will be built on top of the podium, which will be overlooked by the iconic BT Tower structure. Orms has submitted a planning application to transform the BT Tower into a hotel with a rooftop swimming pool Plans also include improving the public space around the building and opening the upper portion of the 177-metre-tall tower to the public for the first time since 1981. "Our vision has always been to honour the BT Tower's remarkable history while reimagining its future," said MCR CEO Tyler Morse. "Submitting our planning application is an exciting step towards reopening this landmark after almost 50 years, revitalising the area with new jobs and open space for Camden." Read: Richard and Su Rogers' seminal house in London "gifted to the nation" Originally designed by the Ministry of Public Building and Works, led by chief architects Eric Bedford and G R Yeats, the communications tower opened in 1964 as the Post Office Tower. Designed to support microwave aerials, which were removed in 2011, the distinctive structure was topped by a revolving restaurant that closed in the early 1980s. The BT Tower was the tallest building in London when it was built and retained the title until the NatWest Tower was built in 1980. MCR first announced its acquisition of the tower in 2024. At the time, UK practice Heatherwick Studio was set to lead the transformation of the building into a hotel. Orms took over the project earlier this year. Works are expected to commence in 2029, once the building has been fully vacated, and MCR plans for the transformation to be completed and open to the public by 2033. items.text: Yarlington Lodge blends "little snippets of history with life today" Magazine Awards Jobs Events Guide Showroom School Shows Courses Competitions Follow: Architecture Interiors Design Technology Series Features Interviews Opinion News Lookbooks Talks Videos Podcasts About Comments Newsletters Preferences Submit a story Advertise Privacy notice Contact Dezeen Magazine dezeen-logo dezeen-logo Next story clear Search --> --> Follow: Awards Jobs Events Guide Showroom School Shows Courses Competitions Series Interviews Opinion Talks Videos Newsletters Podcasts Magazine Architecture Interiors Design Technology --> Search results: Read more: Posts: --> Refine your search: Cats Yarlington Lodge at The Newt in Somerset blends "little snippets of history with life today" Share: Prefer Dezeen on Google Jane Englefield | 24 August 2026 British studio Richard Parr Associates has renovated a trio of 19th-century buildings at The Newt in Somerset hotel in England , restoring their interiors to nod to the site's past. Named Yarlington Lodge , the buildings are spread across five hectares of rural land at The Newt in Somerset , a luxury estate, hotel and working farm located just outside of Bruton. Yarlington Lodge is a three-building holiday home at The Newt in Somerset Conceived by Richard Parr Associates as a 32-guest holiday home, the project comprises the main lodge, the Coach House and the Cottage in the Wall – three buildings that historically served as a rectory, its coach house and the gardener's cottage, respectively. "They were once a functioning trio and we wanted them to become so again," studio founder Richard Parr told Dezeen. Patterns and bright colours reference the Napoleonic era in the main lodge The architect worked with The Newt in Somerset's founders, Koos Bekker and Karen Roos, to restore each property. For the 1831 lodge, striking patterns and bright colours were selected to reference the high drama of the Napoleonic era . The Coach House was renovated to reflect its equestrian history Bedroom ceilings were clad with swooping textiles that give the impression of military tents, while classical paintings embellish the green-hued library. Despite these statement design features, Parr explained that interventions to the bones of each building were intentionally subtle. This included carefully restoring the lodge's old fireplaces, elm floorboards and stonework. "Deliberately pared-back" changes were made to the facades "Houses need to retain the spirit of their entire life and should reflect their many owners, hence the references to previous occupants through portraiture and furniture," said the architect. "The renovation is a mix of little snippets of history with life today," he added. A swimming pool also features within the grounds The Coach House was also adapted to reflect its equestrian history. Blackened steel and raw timber characterise the interior spaces, including the brick-clad living room with a low-slung, beam-lined ceiling. B

KTGY 's Interiors Studio was brought on to refresh the detailing and bring light into the dark spaces of the hotel, with a focus on the premium rooms and lounges. In total, the studio renovated 83 rooms, as well as meeting rooms and a terrace on the second level. KTGY has revamped the Fairmont Chicago Millennium Park hotel Originally designed by global studio HOK in the 1980s, the postmodern skyscraper hotel in Chicago's Millennium Park neighbourhood features a rationalised structure with neoclassical columns at the base. At the top, it's crowned by an oxidised copper turret that recalls the distinct châteauesque style of Fairmont hotels. However, the elongated body gives the building a sense of verticality more akin to a modern skyscraper, with the mix of the historical and industrial contributing to the "postmodern" descriptions of the building. The scope included lounges and premium rooms The studio said that the primary reason behind the renovation was reflecting aspects of the postmodern skyscraper's facade in the interior, bringing the details down to scale. "KTGY's interiors team reflected the building's postmodern architectural style by bringing that prominence down to a human scale," said the team. Read: Tatjana von Stein blends Jugendstil style with 1980s glamour for The Dean Munich This included the uncovering of previously concealed architectural details, such as in the Rouge meeting room, where KTGY revealed windows and raised a sunken floor. Here and throughout, the team integrated a visual palette that is modern while retaining some of the decadent detailing – such as an abstract chandelier and a textural sideboard, flanked by roped-LED sconces. The finishes and interior architecture were updated to lighten up the spaces In the 15th-floor lounge, the studio completely redid the finishes and flooring and placed a library area to make the space feel more homey. On the second-floor terrace, patterned wood flooring meets fluted wall details painted a matte green. KTGY wanted to reference the architecture of the 1980s postmodern skyscraper The rooms them

items.title: Photos reveal world's tallest hotel in Dubai
items.text: Photos reveal world's tallest hotel in Dubai Magazine Awards Jobs Events Guide Showroom School Shows Courses Competitions Follow: Architecture Interiors Design Technology Series Features Interviews Opinion News Lookbooks Talks Videos Podcasts About Comments Newsletters Preferences Submit a story Advertise Privacy notice Contact Dezeen Magazine dezeen-logo dezeen-logo Next story clear Search --> --> Follow: Awards Jobs Events Guide Showroom School Shows Courses Competitions Series Interviews Opinion Talks Videos Newsletters Podcasts Magazine Architecture Interiors Design Technology --> Search results: Read more: Posts: --> Refine your search: Cats Photos reveal world's tallest hotel in Dubai Share: Prefer Dezeen on Google Amy Peacock | 21 August 2026 Photographer Ahmad Alnaji has captured the Ciel Dubai Marina, a supertall skyscraper by architecture studio NORR that was recently completed as the tallest hotel in the world. Ciel Dubai Marina opened in November last year, rising 377 metres to beat the 356-metre-tall Gevora Hotel, also in Dubai , as the world's tallest hotel-only building. Ciel Dubai Marina is the tallest hotel-only building in the world Alnaji, founder of photography studio Sarab , was commissioned by NORR project lead Yahya Jan to capture the Ciel Dubai Marina as the architect "intended it to be seen". "Jan wanted photos that are artistic yet don't deceive the viewer about the true design and elements of Ciel," Alnaji told Dezeen. "The photos are made to tell the story of a unique architectural icon." An opening cuts through the upper portion of the skyscraper Operated by IHG's Vignette Collection hotels, Ciel Dubai Marina contains 1,004 hotel rooms, eight cafes and restaurants, a spa, gym, and amenities for children. Built atop a white-clad podium, the skyscraper has a tapering form that narrows at the top and bottom, with curved facades clad in cold-bent glass panels designed to reflect prevailing winds. Read: Ten record-breaking skyscrapers from around the world Evocative of the eye of a needle, an opening in the upper portion of the 82-storey skyscraper contains an infinity pool on the 76th floor overlooking the surrounding Dubai Marina. The opening is bridged above by a publicly accessible observation deck, while below, a 300-metre-tall atrium split into a series of terraces forms the spine of the skyscraper. Ciel Dubai Marina rises 377 metres tall "Inside, the architecture centres on a 300-metre atrium cut through the tower's core, holding vertically stacked, landscaped sky gardens with naturally ventilated terraces spaced through the height of the building," said Alnaji "These are Jan's answer to vertical living, daylit communal voids that bring planting and shared space into a supertall hotel rather than stacking rooms alone." NORR designed a series of shared terraces in the hotel Founded in 1938, NORR is an architecture, engineering and planning studio with offices in cities across Canada, the USA and the UK. Located in a 1928 beaux-arts building on New York City's famous Park Avenue, Kimpton Ashbel was designed to feel like a private residence. A neutral colour palette is juxtaposed with jewel tones at Kimpton Ashbel "Park Avenue is one of New York City's most iconic streets, instantly evoking the elegance of its heritage townhouses," Busta Studio founder Anna Busta told Dezeen. "Drawing from this distinctive spirit, we envisioned a conceptual townhouse experience – welcoming guests into a warm, elegantly curated home." Artworks decorate both guestrooms and communal areas Anna and her husband Jonathan Busta, who run Busta Studio together, used hand-brushed blonde limed oak panelling and arches juxtaposed with Bianco Dolomiti and Pietra marbles to create the right feel for the interior. The studio also combined hand-cast bronze, glass, inlaid bronze and hand-cut mosaic stone with white plaster ceilings and mouldings for a deliberately simple yet elegant look. "The New York townhouse concept itself is an endless source of inspiration: a place where one lingers, surrounded by bespoke millwork, refined finishes, stylish furnishings, and a curated mix of art and collected objects that feel personal and storied," Jonathan Busta told Dezeen. The hotel was designed to feel like a home To create privacy from the bustle of Park Avenue, custom louvres were added at street level. Guests are welcomed by a custom inlaid mosaic featuring the hotel's KA initials when entering the lobby, which Busta Studio filled with specially commissioned artworks and decorative objects. The studio, headed by Alessio Nardi and Lukas Persakovas, was tasked with renovating the Victorian building that was originally converted into a hotel in 1999. A-nrd transformed this 19th-century Glasgow townhouse into a hotel British hospitality brand Oberland wanted its debut hotel to reflect its low intervention approach to development, so A-nrd began by stripping away layers of additions to reveal the building's original fabric. "From the outset, we wanted Arthouse to feel like a place that had always belonged to the city," Nardi explained. "Every decision was made with the existing architecture in mind, from restoring original features and designing bespoke furniture to collaborating with Scottish artists, makers and craftspeople." The original birdcage lift, stained-glass windows and tiled walls were carefully preserved In a previous incarnation the hotel was known as the ArtHouse so the team chose to revive this identity and reinforce the connection to the site’s history. The reimagined interior seeks to balance the building's grandeur with a more intimate atmosphere inspired by the spontaneity and casual decor of an artist's atelier. Original wooden floorboards were left exposed The original birdcage lift, stained-glass windows and tiled walls were carefully preserved and restored as part of the project, while the Victorian proportions and high ceilings lend the spaces a generous feel. Elements such as the original brick walls and wooden floors were left exposed and any necessary repairs were made using modern materials to create an intentional contrast between old and new. The 76 guest rooms combine original features with contemporary interventions made for the project "Glasgow has a strong industrial heritage that we wanted to reference in this project," Nardi told Dezeen. items.title: Joyce Wang draws on "colonial country manors" for Hong Kong hotel interior
items.text: Joyce Wang draws on "colonial country manors" for Hong Kong hotel Magazine Awards Jobs Events Guide Showroom School Shows Courses Competitions Follow: Architecture Interiors Design Technology Series Features Interviews Opinion News Lookbooks Talks Videos Podcasts About Comments Newsletters Preferences Submit a story Advertise Privacy notice Contact Dezeen Magazine dezeen-logo dezeen-logo Next story clear Search --> --> Follow: Awards Jobs Events Guide Showroom School Shows Courses Competitions Series Interviews Opinion Talks Videos Newsletters Podcasts Magazine Architecture Interiors Design Technology --> Search results: Read more: Posts: --> Refine your search: Cats Joyce Wang draws on "colonial country manors" for Hong Kong hotel interior Share: Prefer Dezeen on Google Christina Yao | 4 August 2026 Designer Joyce Wang has completed an interior renovation at the Mandarin Oriental The Landmark hotel in Hong Kong, designed to evoke the feel of living in a colonial mansion. Located on Queen's Road in Hong Kong's Central district, the hotel was first established a decade ago. It recently reopened after the completion of interior renovation by Joyce Wang Studio and a new facade design by Neri&Hu . Terracotta tones in the lobby nod to Hong Kong's colonial architecture Joyce Wang Studio referenced Hong Kong’s historic architecture and skyline when designing the hotel, whose interior was informed by the city's colonial country manors. "We took inspiration from the colonial country manors frequented by the Tai Pans of a bygone era to celebrate the beauty of these historic homes that still fascinate today," Wang, principal of her eponymous studio, told Dezeen. "Our vision this time has a greater focus on local relevance and the heritage of the building." The studio also aimed to fuse art into the hotel . "We also used art as an integral part of our philosophy for the space, with a commitment to adding local flavour. The artwork program is rigorous in that there is a story behind each piece," Wang added. Undulating staircase extends around a large-scale contemporary artwork The hotel lobby features a mix of materials including stone, timber and textured wallcoverings. Custom eglomisé glass was added as detailing to create a contemporary atmosphere. Terracotta tones within the space nod to Hong Kong's colonial architecture and were combined with a touch of green and orange in response to the city's lush green parks. When designing the project, NM3 drew on the influential design of Loos's famous bar , an early modernist landmark finished in 1908. Bar Bardo was designed by NM3 "The American Bar was more of an aspiration than a direct formal reference," studio co-founder Francesco Zorzi told Dezeen. "The ambition was never to recreate Loos's bar, nor Robert and Trix Haussmann's Kronenhalle in Zurich, which was another important reference for the project," he explained. "Rather, we wanted to create a truly classic bar for Milan, with a very specific spatial and architectural character." The studio was informed by Adolf Loos's famous American Bar in Vienna Located just across the road from the city's popular Bar Basso , Bar Bardo is housed within a 55-square-metre single room with an additional bathroom. Almost every element in the listening bar was custom-designed by NM3, known for its modernist-style stainless steel furniture that has already made the young studio a household name in Milan since its founding in 2020. Polished rosewood panels clad the walls and ceilings The walls and ceiling were clad with polished rosewood panels, which add character to the small space while improving its acoustics. A quintessentially NM3 stainless steel bar was placed in the centre of the room, where its gleaming surfaces reflect the globular 1950s pendant lights by Italian architect Luigi Caccia Dominioni. The lamps are the only vintage pieces in the bar. NM3 swapped their original chains with longer black ones. Named after Greenspan 's daughter Vivienne, VV's Cocktail Room (VV's) is located in Chelsea and contains just 18 seats to mimic the intimacy of an omakase cocktail experience, where bartenders lead a multi-course tasting or cocktail menu. items.title: Fabio Fantolino looks to 1960s offices for interior of retro Turin bar
items.text: Fabio Fantolino looks to 1960s offices for interior of retro Turin bar Magazine Awards Jobs Events Guide Showroom School Shows Courses Competitions Follow: Architecture Interiors Design Technology Series Features Interviews Opinion News Lookbooks Talks Videos Podcasts About Comments Newsletters Preferences Submit a story Advertise Privacy notice Contact Dezeen Magazine dezeen-logo dezeen-logo Next story clear Search --> --> Follow: Awards Jobs Events Guide Showroom School Shows Courses Competitions Series Interviews Opinion Talks Videos Newsletters Podcasts Magazine Architecture Interiors Design Technology --> Search results: Read more: Posts: --> Refine your search: Cats Fabio Fantolino looks to 1960s offices for interior of retro Turin bar Share: Prefer Dezeen on Google Alice Laycock | 29 June 2026 Cantilever chairs , wood panelling and mirror -clad surfaces meet in Lève Office Bar, a Space Age-informed bar in Turin by Italian architect Fabio Fantolino . The venue is located in the centre of the Italian city and nods to the aesthetics and culture of workplaces built in post-war America. A stainless steel bar sets the tone upon entry The original building dates from the 1920s and before the intervention, it was divided into two distinct units: one contained a cafe, while the other housed a bookshop. It now functions as one cohesive interior subdivided into three spaces, all of which reference retro workplaces. Herringbone bricks give way to green resin flooring beyond The space aims to serve professionals working in the city centre over the course of a typical working day; hence the architect's decision to theme it around retro offices. "The 1960s were chosen as the reference period because they marked a time when offices were regarded as prestigious and carefully designed workplaces – the 'office bar' concept, on the other hand, reflects the way we work today," Fantolino told Dezeen. "It is conceived as a space that supports the everyday rhythm of contemporary office life, whether for breakfast, lunch, coffee breaks, or aperitivos, while also acknowledging that work can naturally extend into hospitality spaces." All the fittings and fixtures were selected according to 1960s aesthetics "The three areas reinterpret the concept of an open-plan office, each through a distinct design language," Fantolino continued. A monolithic stainless-steel bar dominates the initial interior upon entry. Its strong presence is bolstered by a red enamel wall panel mounted behind it. The ceiling beneath the mezzanine presents a mirrored alternative to conventional grid ceilings The effect is softened by a herringbone floor made up of sandy-coloured bricks, which gives way to a green resin floor at the threshold of the second space. Banquette seating upholstered in fawn-coloured leather runs along the far wall, accompanied by red-topped cafe tables and brown-and-chrome cantilever chairs. Focacha is the latest venue from hospitality specialist Grupo La Confitería, which tasked Serra 's studio with creating a space that pays tribute to an important period in the history of Barcelona's nightlife. Isern Serra has designed a Barcelona bar with multi-coloured modular furniture that evokes Verner Panton pieces The 1960s and early 1970s coincided with the heyday of Tuset Street where the bar is located, which became a hub for a group of young liberal professionals known in Barcelona art the "gauche divine". The cocktail bar was designed to evoke the futuristic styling that characterised this time and immerse guests in a multi-sensory environment defined by design, light and music. The bar is hidden behind the facade of a traditional focacceria "I wanted visitors to feel enveloped by an environment with a strong artistic and emotional presence, capable of sparking curiosity and creating a sense of wonder from the very first moment," Serra told Dezeen. "More than designing a cocktail bar, the intention was to create a setting that evokes emotions, encourages contemplation and leaves a lasting impression on those who experience it, turning their visit into something truly memorable." Visitors enter through a refrigerator inside the shop The speakeasy-style venue is hidden behind the facade of a traditional focacceria that has been serving Italian bread for 50 years. Visitors enter through a refrigerator inside the shop, which adds a sense of theatricality to the experience. The venue was divided into two spaces, the first of which is a bar that pays homage to Danish designer Panton's iconic Visiona installations. items.title: Wild Form designs with "no straight lines" for bar next to New York's Stonewall Inn
items.text: Wild Form designs bar with "no straight lines" next to Stonewall Inn Magazine Awards Jobs Events Guide Showroom School Shows Courses Competitions Follow: Architecture Interiors Design Technology Series Features Interviews Opinion News Lookbooks Talks Videos Podcasts About Comments Newsletters Preferences Submit a story Advertise Privacy notice Contact Dezeen Magazine dezeen-logo dezeen-logo Next story clear Search --> --> Follow: Awards Jobs Events Guide Showroom School Shows Courses Competitions Series Interviews Opinion Talks Videos Newsletters Podcasts Magazine Architecture Interiors Design Technology --> Search results: Read more: Posts: --> Refine your search: Cats Wild Form designs with "no straight lines" for bar next to New York's Stonewall Inn Share: Prefer Dezeen on Google Dan Howarth | 27 June 2026 New York-based Wild Form Design Studio has crafted a sculptural interior for a bar called Love Thy Neighbor, which "celebrates the queer community" next to The Stonewall Inn in the West Village . Opened ahead of this weekend’s Pride celebrations in New York, Love Thy Neighbor sits next to the landmark where a series of protests in 1969 became a pivotal moment in mobilising the Gay Rights Movement. The bar features free-form shapes that nod to queerness and individuality Founders Shigefumi Kabashima and Elias Popa, along with Wild Form Design Studio , wanted the bar and dining concept to pay homage to the history of this location, both through design and their approach to hospitality. "Guided by the ethos of no straight lines, Love Thy Neighbor celebrates the queer community, chosen family, and the joys of gathering and belonging," said the team. Shelves behind the bar follow the "no straight lines" rule set out by the owners Just over the below-grade threshold, a concrete floor panel is gilded with a quote from Marsha P Johnson – a transgender woman who was a key figure in the Stonewall Uprising protests for LGBTQ+ rights, and who continued to fight for queer rights and representation throughout her life. It reads "No pride for some of us without liberation for all of us" in gold letters and includes her signature below. A series of banquettes is divided by sculptural partitions A single brick from the original Stonewall Inn is displayed in a niche at the end of the bar, representing those thrown at the police who raided the bar on 28 June 1969 during the uprisings. "These elements serve as understated reminders of the past, while reinforcing a bright future ahead," said the team. A single brick from the original Stonewall Inn is displayed in a niche Elsewhere, the curvaceous walls and partitions form an intimate, cavern-like space for 40 guests, and nod to queerness and individuality. "The idea of 'no straight lines' became a guiding principle for us," said Kabashima. "It reflects not only the design of the space, but also how we think about hospitality: fluid, open, and without boundaries." Spotlights illuminate the bar counter and tables

Occupying the basement levels of a building in Marylebone, Dive features furniture and materials that adapt to different scenarios and celebrate signs of use. Golem has designed the interiors for Marylebone bar Dive "Dive's experience is an ongoing negotiation between the design and its guests," explained Golem founder Ariel André. "The bar is not finished at opening, it is finished nightly, by hands, shoes, spills." "Wear and tear is part of the architecture," he added. "Glossy surfaces are designed to take scratches from glasses and jewellery, velvety walls and floors are meant to retain the imprint of bodies." The bar is covered almost entirely in red velvet Dive's owner chose to divide the venue into two distinct zones: a luminous bar area near the entrance and a darker, more intimate lounge reached by descending a short flight of steps. Clean lines and sculptural forms define the bar, which features a curved cutout along its front. Convex mirrors and surfaces rendered in smooth, glossy finishes reflect light and movement throughout the space. The fabric retains "the imprint of bodies" "The palette and shimmering light are calibrated for a transitional feel, somewhere between dusk and dawn: warm enough to flatter skin tones, restrained enough to leave the shimmering cocktails in focus," André explained. A dark corridor leads to the steps that descend into the richer, more tactile lounge space. This area was designed to facilitate moments of interaction between guests, while also offering cosy corners for private conversations. Structural arches supporting the street above contain flexible seating areas that can be configured to suit various social scenarios. Built-in benches lining the niches are covered with loose cushions that can be repositioned as required. "The upholstery is conceived to be appropriated by guests," André pointed out. "Bodies shape the furniture, not the other way around." "When unoccupied, the seating still carries the imprint of previous guests, holding the ev

The team has completely redesigned Peak with Priceless , the restaurant located on the 101th floor of the KPF-designed 30 Hudson Yards skyscraper. The interiors of Peak by Priceless have been redesigned so every seat has an uninterrupted skyline view The overhaul also includes the addition of Avenue Sky Lounge – a revival of the popular Avenue nightclub in Chelsea, which shuttered in 2020 due to the Covid-19 pandemic and never reopened. Susan Nugraha, Tao Group Hospitality 's SVP of design and development, worked closely on the project with experiential design group Journey . Custom tiered lighting nods to art deco skyscrapers such as the Empire State Building Both hospitality concepts draw design influences from the Manhattan skyline visible through the wraparound, floor-to-ceiling windows. "The inspiration behind Peak and Avenue was always New York itself, its energy, glamour and unmistakable sense of occasion," said Journey managing director David Taglione. "Suspended above the city with the skyline as its stage, we wanted to create a hospitality experience that feels both elevated and deeply connected to the rhythm of New York." Soft blue and warm brown suede covers the booth seating References to art deco structures such as the Empire State Building and Rockefeller Center can be spied in tall, tiered lamps, customised to softly illuminate both Peak and Avenue spaces. "Every design decision, from the rich materiality to the layered seating and subtle Art Deco references, was shaped to frame the view while creating a space with its own distinct sense of presence," said Taglione.
